title: Rook against two connected pawns
summary: When two pawns beat the rook, how rook and king stop them, and counting the tempi.
part.sixth.title: On the sixth, the pawns win
part.sixth.summary: With no kings nearby, two connected pawns on the sixth rank are stronger than the rook.
part.fifth.title: On the fifth, the move decides
part.fifth.summary: One step earlier, the rook alone still wins, if it is its move and it attacks from the side.
part.king.title: The rook's king counts the squares
part.king.summary: With your king close, the rook wins even against pawns on the sixth. One square farther, and it loses.
part.escort.title: The king escorts the pawns
part.escort.summary: The other side: the king hides from the checks and the right pawn advances.
part.resource.title: Mating threats
part.resource.summary: When the pawns have already arrived, the rook can still draw by threatening the black king on the edge.
part.recap.title: Summary
part.recap.summary: Three rules and the ending against the machine.
step.t_sixth: Black's pawns are already on their sixth rank, and neither king is close. The white rook is to move. Can it stop both?
step.t_sixth.hint1: Try each rook move and see what the other pawn does in reply.
step.t_sixth.hint2: If the rook stands in front of one pawn, the other one moves. If it attacks both, one advances, guarded by the other.
step.sixth: It can't. Each pawn is two steps from promoting, and as soon as one advances, the other guards it. If the rook goes to f1, the g-pawn advances; if it goes to g1, the f-pawn does. If it takes a pawn, the other one is already through. Here every White move loses. The kings on a8 and h8 take no part: it is the rook alone against the two pawns, and at this point the pawns are stronger.
step.d_sixth: Watch the duel from Black's side. The rook tries both files, and the pawns always answer with the other one.
step.d_sixth.m1: Rf1: the rook stands in front of the f-pawn.
step.d_sixth.m2: g2! The other pawn moves. Now it threatens to queen on g1.
step.d_sixth.m3: Rg1: the rook rushes in front of the g-pawn.
step.d_sixth.m4: f2! The pawn attacks the rook on g1 and threatens to queen on f1.
step.d_sixth.m5: Rxg2: the rook takes one pawn...
step.d_sixth.m6: ...and the other one queens. Queen against rook, and Black wins.
step.euwe: Max Euwe, a world champion, taught a rule of thumb: two connected pawns on the sixth are worth a rook. In this position you can see the count: added together, the squares the two pawns still need are only four. Even with Black to move, the rook can't hold. Notice it is the reverse of what you just saw: here the pawns are White's and the rook is Black's. The rule works both ways.
step.push: Now you play the pawns. The rook has attacked both along the third rank. Don't waste time with the king: push.
step.push.hint: f2 or g2: the pawn that moves is guarded by the other one. Then the other pawn runs too.
step.push.done: A new queen. The rook was late to every square: with the pawns on the sixth, each of their moves is a threat, and the rook can only answer one.
step.t_fifth: Now the pawns are one step back, on the fifth. The kings are still far away, and the rook is to move. Is there a winning move?
step.t_fifth.hint1: In the last position the pawns needed only two steps. Here they need three. The rook has one tempo to spare.
step.t_fifth.hint2: Look for a square from which the rook attacks both pawns at once.
step.fifth: Ra4! The rook goes to the pawns' rank and attacks both from the side. The g-pawn is stuck: if it advances, the rook takes the f-pawn and the g-pawn is left alone. If the f-pawn advances, the g-pawn falls. And if Black does nothing, the rook takes on f4. Either way one pawn is left alone, and a lone pawn the rook catches from behind. It is the only move: anything else draws or loses.
step.fifthTempo: The same position, but Black is to move. Now a pawn reaches the sixth before the rook gets organised: after f3, the rook can win only one of the pawns, and the other, with the black king helping, is enough for a draw. On the fifth rank, whoever has the move decides. That is why this ending is counted, not guessed.
step.fifthMove: Your turn: attack the pawns from the side and collect what is left.
step.fifthMove.hint: Ra4, on the pawns' rank. After Kg7, Rxf4. After g3, the rook goes back to the g-file.
step.fifthMove.done: One pawn has fallen and the rook has the other under control. Now just bring the king and finish it off.
step.t_king: The pawns are back on the sixth, but now your king is on c4, not on a8. The rook alone was losing. And with the king nearby?
step.t_king.hint1: Count how many moves your king needs to stand next to the squares the pawns will pass.
step.t_king.hint2: The pawns need two moves to reach the first rank. The rook on a1 already watches that whole rank.
step.king: With the king close, the rook wins. It stays where it is, guarding the first rank, and the king runs diagonally: Kd3 and then Ke2 or Ke3, next to the pawns. Together, king and rook do what the rook alone couldn't: the king guards the promotion squares the rook doesn't cover and attacks the pawns up close. Fine and Benko sum it up: with the rook's king far away, two pawns win; with it close, the rook wins.
step.kingLate: Now the same position with the king one square to the side, on b4. It looks like nothing, but it is one more move to e2, and the pawns don't wait: after Rc3 f2, both pawns arrive before the king. It loses. In this ending you count square by square, as in the king's race against a pawn.
step.d_king: Watch the king arrive in time. Notice the rook doesn't move: it is already doing its job on a1.
step.d_king.m1: Kd3: diagonally, towards the squares in front of the pawns.
step.d_king.m2: g2: the pawn threatens g1, but the rook covers that square.
step.d_king.m3: Ke3! The king attacks f3 and watches f2. The pawns are frozen.
step.d_king.m4: Kg7: the black king tries to come, but it is too far away.
step.d_king.m7: Kxg2: the second pawn. King and rook against king: the rest is technique.
step.kingMove: Now your king is on c3. Count the squares and arrive in time.
step.kingMove.hint: Kd2: always towards e2. After f2, Ke2, and then the rook attacks the g-pawn.
step.kingMove.done: Just in time. The king holds f1 and the f-pawn, and the rook takes care of the rest. Note that Kc2 or Kb3 lost: only the moves that bring the king closer to the pawns win.
step.t_escort: Switch sides: now you have the pawns, with your king close, and the black king is far away. The black rook will give checks. What is the way to promote?
step.t_escort.hint1: If you push g6 at once, see which check the rook gives and what it gains.
step.t_escort.hint2: Look for a square for the king where the rook can't reach it with checks, and only then push.
step.escort: Haste ruins everything. If g6, Rh5+! and the rook gains the time it needed: a draw. The king first needs shelter: on h7, in front of the h-pawn, the rook can't check along the h-file, and the g-pawn is free to run. It is the king that escorts the pawns, not the other way round.
step.d_escort: Watch the king go to its shelter before the pawns move.
step.d_escort.m1: Kg6! The king protects both pawns and heads for h7.
step.d_escort.m2: Kc7: the black king runs, but it is too far.
step.d_escort.m3: Kh7: the shelter. The rook has no check, because the h-pawn blocks the file.
step.d_escort.m7: g7, and g8 comes next. The rook would have to give itself up for the pawn.
step.escortMove: The same on the other side of the board. Shelter the king, and only then push.
step.escortMove.hint: Kb6, then Ka7, in front of the a-pawn. Only then b6.
step.escortMove.done: The king on a7 blocks the a-file and guards b8. The black rook has no checks, and the b-pawn walks all the way.
step.t_resource: Black already has the pawns on the sixth and their king is close to the edge. The rook alone can't stop the pawns. Is there a way out?
step.t_resource.hint1: Look at the black king, not at the pawns. Where is it, and where is your king?
step.t_resource.hint2: A check on the g-file, with your king nearby, pushes the black king to the edge.
step.resource: The pawns can't be stopped any more. But the black king is right next to the h-file, and your king is very close to it. Rc1! prepares Rg1+, and after Kh4 your king goes to f4: now the threat is Rh1, mate. The black king has to flee the threats instead of helping the pawns, and White repeats the threats until the draw.
step.d_resource: Watch how the white rook and king make Black go round in circles.
step.d_resource.m1: Rc1! The rook goes to the first rank, on its way to g1.
step.d_resource.m3: Rg1+: the black king goes to the edge.
step.d_resource.m5: Kf4! Now Rh1 would be mate. The black king has no time for the pawns.
step.d_resource.m7: Kf3! The same threat, one rank lower.
step.d_resource.m8: Kh4: the king comes back, and White repeats. A draw.
step.resourceTrap: Watch the trap on the other side: if at the end the black king goes to h2 instead of h4, it escapes the threats, but it also abandons the pawns. Ra1! and the rook goes back to them: it takes a2, then b2. The black king must stay close to your king for the draw to hold.
step.resourceMove: The rook is now on c7. Find the way out and hold the draw.
step.resourceMove.hint: Rc1, on the way to the g-file. After a2, Rg1+. After Kh4, Kf4.
step.resourceMove.done: A draw. The rook didn't stop the pawns; the mating threats took Black's time away.
step.recap: Three rules for your games. First: two connected pawns on the sixth, with no kings nearby, beat the rook. Before that, on the fifth, the rook that has the move attacks both from the side and wins.
step.rules: Second: the rook's king changes everything, but it must arrive in time, and that is counted square by square, diagonally. Third: on the pawns' side, the king hides from the checks before the pawn moves; on the rook's side, when the pawns are already through, look for mating threats.
step.recapMove: One last time, on the other side of the board: the pawns are on the fifth and the rook is to move.
step.recapMove.hint: Rh4, on the pawns' rank. After Kb7, Rxc4.
step.recapMove.done: That's it. Attack from the side, and the pawn that is left is alone.
step.finish: Now against the machine, in the position with your king on c4. Count the squares, don't let the rook leave the first rank too early, and win.
ex.e01: White to play and win. The pawns are on the fifth and the kings are far away. Where does the rook attack?
ex.e01.hint: The rook must attack both pawns at the same time.
ex.e01.solution: Rb4! On the pawns' rank, the rook attacks both. If one advances, the other falls, and the one left is alone. Any other move lets a pawn reach the sixth and only draws.
ex.e02: White to play and win. The pawns are on the sixth, but your king is close. Which way does it go?
ex.e02.hint: The rook already watches the first rank. The king must get next to the pawns.
ex.e02.solution: Ke4 (or Kd4, or the check Rh1+ first): diagonally, towards e3 and f2. With the king there and the rook on a1, the pawns are stuck. Ke5 or Kc4 look similar, but they arrive one tempo late and lose.
ex.e03: White to play and win. The pawns are on the sixth and your king is far from them. Take a good look at the black king.
ex.e03.hint: The black king is in the corner. What happens if your king gets close to it?
ex.e03.solution: Kf7! The black king is trapped in the corner, and the rook threatens a check on the h-file that is mate. For example, g2 Ra4 Kh7 Rh4, mate. Black has no time to promote. Any other move loses: the pawns are too fast.
ex.e04: Black to play and win. The white rook has gone in front of the f-pawn. What is the plan?
ex.e04.hint: On the sixth, every tempo belongs to the pawns. Don't spend it on the king.
ex.e04.solution: g2 (or f2): one pawn advances and the rook can't deal with both. If the rook goes to g1, f2 attacks the rook and threatens f1. A king move, on the other hand, gives the rook the time it needed and loses.
ex.e05: White to play and win. The pawns are not both on the sixth yet. How does the rook attack them?
ex.e05.hint: One rook square attacks the g-pawn from behind and the f-pawn from the side.
ex.e05.solution: Rg4! The rook attacks f4 and, along the file, the pawn on g3. If g2, Rxg2, and the f-pawn is alone with the black king far away. Attack before both reach the sixth.
ex.e06: Black to play and win. The pawns are well advanced. Pawn or king?
ex.e06.hint: With the rook behind the pawns, the king is the one that must help first.
ex.e06.solution: Ka2! The king comes in front of the a-pawn and guards b3 and b2. Now the b-pawn walks with an escort. If a2 instead, White brings the king in time and it is a draw. It is the idea of Audax6's study: the king before the pawns.
ex.e07: White to play and win. This is the position from Shankland against Maghsoodloo, Prague 2022. What would you play?
ex.e07.hint: The most advanced pawn is not the one that should move now. Think about the black rook's checks.
ex.e07.solution: Ka7! (Kb7 also wins). The king goes in front of the a-pawn, where the rook can't reach it, and the b-pawn advances later. Shankland played Ka7. The tempting a7? allows Ra2! and the black king arrives in time: a draw.
ex.e08: White to play and draw. The pawns are already on the sixth and the black king is near the edge. What is the resource?
ex.e08.hint: The rook won't stop the pawns. It needs to reach a check that drives the black king into the corner.
ex.e08.solution: Rd1! The rook goes to the first rank, ready for Rg1+. Then your king approaches the black one and threatens Rh1, mate. The other moves lose: the pawns run through while the rook is looking at them.
ex.e09: White to play and win. The pawns are on the sixth, but your rook and your king are on the same rank as the black king. One move gains a whole tempo.
ex.e09.hint: When the king steps out of the rook's way, who gives the check?
ex.e09.solution: Kd4+! A discovered check from the rook on c5. The black king must answer, and your king has already gained a step towards the pawns. After Kf4, Kc3 (or Rc1, or Rc4) and the king arrives in time. On the first move, Rc1 only draws, and the other moves lose.
ex.e11: White to play and win. Your king is far away and every move counts. Find the three king moves.
ex.e11.hint: Diagonally, always towards the e2 square.
ex.e11.solution: Kc4!, after g3, Kd3!, and after Kg4, Ke2!. Three only moves: the king reaches e2, holds f1, and the rook does the rest. Kc5 or Kb4 on the first move already only draw.
key.sixth: On the sixth, the pawns win: every White move loses. Own position, illustrating Euwe and Meiden's rule quoted on Wikipedia.
key.fifth: On the fifth, only Ra4 wins; with Black to move, a draw. Own position.
key.king: With the king on c4, the rook wins; on b4, it loses. Own position.
key.euwe: Euwe's rule: Black to move can't hold the pawns. From Anki_Thief_of_Crowns's study on Lichess.
key.escort: Kg6! and the king hides on h7. From the Lichess practice, "Rook versus Two Pawns".
key.resource: Rc1! and the mating threats draw. From the Lichess practice, "A Tricky Resource".
history: This ending has no famous discoverer and no name of its own, but it has two rules of thumb that pass from book to book. Max Euwe and Walter Meiden, in The Road to Chess Mastery, wrote that two connected pawns on the sixth are worth a rook. Reuben Fine and Pal Benko, in Basic Chess Endings, added the king to the count: with the rook's king far away, two pawns win; with it close, the rook wins. Jesús de la Villa organises the topic by the kings: neither takes part, only the defender's, or both. It also turns up in grandmaster games. In Shabalov against Friedel, Peabody 2007, the rook's checks drove the pawns' king in front of them and slowed everything down. In Shankland against Maghsoodloo, Prague 2022, Shankland hid his king on a7 before pushing, as you saw in this lesson. The tablebase confirms the rules, and also shows where they fail by a single tempo.
practice: Now against the machine: rook against two pawns on the sixth, with your king close. Count the squares and win.
